If you bought and the contract filled, then the ask quote/price hit your buy-to-open buy limit order.

If the option price (specifically bid quote) rises to your sell-to-close limit order, then it would close out the option and take profits.

And what causes the price of the put to potentially rise to your sell-to-close limit?

2 main things cause that:

1) the price of the stock dropping (the stock heading lower in price/on the chart)

2) volatility – which is the speed of the drop. The quicker the drop, the more the option price expands/grows in value.

It had also had a “throw over” above its recent trading channel and that is typically representative of an overly bullish move that exhausts as “everyone who was dying to buy, has now bought”.

Contrary to what many retail investors think, a “strong uptrend” is not always a good sign, when it starts to show things like I pointed out on this weekly chart (and most investors will never even eye a weekly chart).

Some slams are quick. Some take a while. (Examples in the red boxes).

In the last good slam, the white line measures how stretched it was from the moving average before it collapsed.

You’ll see that same measurement projected onto today’s activity and you can tell that the current JCI move is further stretched from its moving average than the last slam.

So, there is a big potential to see another quick slam downward, but we can’t rule out one that takes some time to get back to the moving averages, because historically those have happened too.

JCI is a prime example of the volatility factor in an option and not just watching what may happen, in time, on the chart.

For instance, JCI has more ultimate downside. However, who would think that the stock takes an almost 3-month pause (or potentially longer) before its next volatile drop?

So, the huge drop lower (first blue line to the left) has both price and volatility benefitting the put.

However, several months of sideways to slightly up action on lesser volatility can shrink back the floating gains made in the blue surge lower and may not re-emerge until the next blue drop downward.

So, it’s why we don’t want to say, “the stock has more downside on its chart, so I’ll stick with the option”. We don’t know how quickly it’ll get to target and the volatility piece is a big factor in factoring the option’s price.

Therefore, when you have huge, favorable surges that put you to your 25% profits, take them or else you may see those floating gains erode away (certainly in instances like this, which will happen sometimes).

Of course, when there’s a huge surge lower and you’re not at a 25% profit, then you do have to ride through the range into the next volatile surge lower.

(Long, boring low-volatile ranges, tend to breakout into highly-volatile directional moves).
